context: The input is [7, 3, 2, 6, 0, 1, 5, 4]. The upper half is labeled “Divide (splitting phase)” and the lower half “Conquer (merging phase).”
description: Keep splitting the current array in half until each subproblem contains one element. The left and right halves do not overlap and can be solved independently. A single element is already sorted without any comparisons.

On return, merge each adjacent pair of sorted results. Compare the first remaining element on each side and take the smaller one. When one side runs out, append the rest of the other. Merging level by level solves the full eight-element problem.

Three levels of splits in the upper half produce eight single elements. Three levels of merges in the lower half produce the sorted result. The table lists the subarrays at all seven levels in the figure.

frames.explanation: The subproblems, like the original problem, involve sorting arrays. The left and right subarrays are independent, and two sorted subarrays can be merged efficiently into one sorted array. These are the features of divide and conquer: a problem can be split into independent subproblems whose solutions can be combined.
frames.title: Divide and conquer in merge sort

summary: Break the eight-element sorting problem down level by level to single-element subproblems. Merge the sorted results from the bottom up to obtain an array in ascending order from 0 to 7.

tables.caption: Levels of splitting and merging
headers: Subarrays in their original left-to-right positions
rows: Merge to solve the original problem
